claim: Toxoplasmosis has been recognized as a leading cause of deaths attributed to foodborne illness in the United States.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is the causative agent of toxoplasmosis, a widespread parasitic disease in humans which has been recognized as leading cause of deaths attributed to foodborne illness in the United States (Scallan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scallan et al., 2015.

claim: Severe to life-threatening toxoplasmosis mainly occurs in immunocompromised people, with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or under chemo- and graft rejection therapies.
source: Severe to life-threatening Toxoplasmosis mainly occur in immunocompromised people, with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or under chemo- and graft rejection therapies (Montoya and Liesenfeld, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Montoya and Liesenfeld, 2004.

claim: Outcomes of congenital toxoplasmosis significantly vary with the timing of infection from recurrent eye diseases to adverse motor or neurologic impairments that can cause stillbirth.
source: In addition, outcomes of congenital toxoplasmosis significantly vary with the timing of infection from recurrent eye diseases to adverse motor or neurologic impairments that can cause stillbirth (Halonen and Weiss, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Halonen and Weiss, 2013.

claim: T. gondii belongs to the protozoan phylum Apicomplexa.
source: T. gondii belongs to the protozoan phylum Apicomplexa and as most Apicomplexa species, develops and proliferates inside a surrogate host cell.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge about T. gondii.

claim: T. gondii can infect virtually all nucleated cells of mammals, marsupials and birds.
source: Remarkably, T. gondii's host range is exceptionally broad since it can infect virtually all nucleated cells of mammals, marsupials and birds (Dubey, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dubey, 2009.

claim: The invasive tachyzoite stage of T. gondii triggers the formation of a unique membrane-bound compartment called the Parasitophorous Vacuole (PV).
source: To achieve intracellular lifestyle, the invasive tachyzoite stage of T. gondii triggers the formation of a unique membrane-bound compartment called the Parasitophorous Vacuole (PV).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. gondii infection mechanism.

claim: The PV is shaped as a niche kept hidden from harmful endocytic processing thereby enabling tachyzoite growth and multiplication.
source: The PV is shaped as a niche kept hidden from harmful endocytic processing thereby enabling tachyzoite growth and multiplication (Jones et al., 1972; Mordue et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones et al., 1972 and Mordue et al., 1999.

claim: GRA18 is a parasite dense granule protein that once released in the host cell cytoplasm forms versatile complexes with regulatory elements of the β-catenin destruction complex.
source: We identified a parasite dense granule protein as GRA18 that once released in the host cell cytoplasm forms versatile complexes with regulatory elements of the β-catenin destruction complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GRA18 drives β-catenin up-regulation and the downstream effects on host cell gene expression by interacting with GSK3/PP2A-B56.
source: By interacting with GSK3/PP2A-B56, GRA18 drives β-catenin up-regulation and the downstream effects on host cell gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the context of macrophages infection, GRA18 induces the expression of a specific set of genes commonly associated with an anti-inflammatory response that includes those encoding chemokines CCL17 and CCL22.
source: In the context of macrophages infection, GRA18 induces the expression of a specific set of genes commonly associated with an anti-inflammatory response that includes those encoding chemokines CCL17 and CCL22.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GRA18 protein accommodates both a signal peptide for targeting to the secretory pathway and a canonical TEXEL motif found on PV residing proteins.
source: GRA18 protein accommodates both a signal peptide for targeting to the secretory pathway and a canonical TEXEL motif found on PV residing proteins (i.e. GRAs proteins), some of which traffic across the PVM to reach the host cell cytoplasm (Coffey et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2017; Hammoudi et al., 2015; Hsiao et al., 2013) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: In extracellular tachyzoites, GRA18-HF partially co-localized with the DG resident protein GRA1 but not with the micronemal protein MIC2 or the toxofilin rhoptry protein.
source: In extracellular tachyzoites, GRA18-HF partially co-localized with the DG resident protein GRA1 but not with the micronemal protein MIC2 or the toxofilin rhoptry protein (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: When expressed in intracellular replicating tachyzoites, the GRA18-HA3 protein accumulated in the cytoplasm of infected cells over time.
source: When expressed in intracellular replicating tachyzoites, the GRA18-HA3 protein accumulated in the cytoplasm of infected cells over time (Figure 1C, upper panel), but was not detected in host cell nucleus in contrast to the yet identified effectors (i.e. PP2C-hn, ROP16, ROP47, GRA16, GRA24, GRA28, and TgIST; for review, see Hakimi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and comparison to known effectors.

claim: GRA18 was not detected in host cell nucleus in contrast to the yet identified effectors (i.e. PP2C-hn, ROP16, ROP47, GRA16, GRA24, GRA28, and TgIST).
source: When expressed in intracellular replicating tachyzoites, the GRA18-HA3 protein accumulated in the cytoplasm of infected cells over time (Figure 1C, upper panel), but was not detected in host cell nucleus in contrast to the yet identified effectors (i.e. PP2C-hn, ROP16, ROP47, GRA16, GRA24, GRA28, and TgIST; for review, see Hakimi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and comparison to known effectors.

claim: In the absence of the parasite MYR1 protein, the export of GRA18 through the PVM no longer occurred.
source: Moreover, in the absence of the parasite MYR1 protein, the export of GRA18 through the PVM no longer occurred (Figure 1D), indicating that GRA18 uses an export pathway shared with the other GRA effectors (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D and citation to Franco et al., 2016.

claim: GRA18 uses an export pathway shared with the other GRA effectors.
source: Moreover, in the absence of the parasite MYR1 protein, the export of GRA18 through the PVM no longer occurred (Figure 1D), indicating that GRA18 uses an export pathway shared with the other GRA effectors (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the MYR1 dependency data and supported by citation to Franco et al., 2016.

claim: GRA18 is a 70 kDa protein predicted to be partially disordered.
source: GRA18 is a 70 kDa protein predicted to be partially disordered (Figure 1E) with no apparent homolog counterpart outside of the Coccidia.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 1E.

claim: GRA18 has no apparent homolog counterpart outside of the Coccidia.
source: GRA18 is a 70 kDa protein predicted to be partially disordered (Figure 1E) with no apparent homolog counterpart outside of the Coccidia.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: GRA18 shows little polymorphism among the three major strain types of T. gondii (99% identity).
source: While GRA18 shows little polymorphism among the three major strain types of T. gondii (99% identity, Figure 1A), the protein is highly divergent in Neospora caninum (39% identity).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GRA18 is highly divergent in Neospora caninum (39% identity).
source: While GRA18 shows little polymorphism among the three major strain types of T. gondii (99% identity, Figure 1A), the protein is highly divergent in Neospora caninum (39% identity).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison.

claim: GRA18 is an additional member of the class of T. gondii DG proteins that are exported in the host cell during tachyzoite life cycle.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that GRA18 is an additional member of the class of T. gondii DG proteins that are exported in the host cell during tachyzoite life cycle (Hakimi et al., 2017; Nadipuram et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented and citations to previous studies.

claim: Multiple components of the β-catenin destruction complex were found among the GRA18 interactants: β-catenin itself, the glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3α/β), and the protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) regulatory subunit B56α/β/γ/δ.
source: Interestingly, multiple components of the β-catenin destruction complex were found among the interactants: β-catenin itself, the glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3α/β), and the protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) regulatory subunit B56α/β/γ/δ (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Following Flag affinity chromatography, GRA18 co-eluted with β-catenin, GSK3α/β, and the PP2A-B56δ/ε within a quite stable complex that resisted to stringent salt and detergent conditions (0.5 M KCl and 0.1% NP-40).
source: Following Flag affinity chromatography, GRA18 co-eluted with β-catenin, GSK3α/β, and the PP2A-B56δ/ε within a quite stable complex that resisted to stringent salt and detergent conditions (0.5 M KCl and 0.1% NP-40) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The identification of the scaffolding subunit PP2A65 RA and the catalytic subunit PP2Ac along with the PP2A-B56, argues for a functional PP2A holoenzyme as part of the complex.
source: Interestingly, the identification of the scaffolding subunit PP2A65 RA and the catalytic subunit PP2Ac along with the PP2A-B56, argues for a functional PP2A holoenzyme as part of the complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mass spectrometry data identifying all three PP2A subunits.

claim: The B56 regulatory subunit presumably mediates the recruitment of the PP2A holoenzyme as it was the only PP2A subunit found by Y2H to interact directly with GRA18.
source: The B56 regulatory subunit presumably mediates the recruitment of the PP2A holoenzyme as it was the only PP2A subunit found by Y2H to interact directly with GRA18 (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Y2H data showing only B56 interacts directly with GRA18.

claim: GRA18 forms distinct complexe(s) with β-catenin, GSK3β, and the PP2A-B56 holoenzyme ranging from 400 to over 700 kDa globular sizes.
source: GRA18 Flag affinity coupled to Size-Exclusion Chromatography (SEC) and immunoblot analysis revealed that GRA18 forms distinct complexe(s) with β-catenin, GSK3β, and the PP2A-B56 holoenzyme ranging from 400 to over 700 kDa globular sizes (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The N-terminal region of GRA18 sheltered the binding site for β-catenin.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal region of GRA18 sheltered the binding site for β-catenin, whereas the C-terminal fragments accommodated the interaction with the PP2A-B56 subunit (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain mapping data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The C-terminal fragments of GRA18 accommodated the interaction with the PP2A-B56 subunit.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal region of GRA18 sheltered the binding site for β-catenin, whereas the C-terminal fragments accommodated the interaction with the PP2A-B56 subunit (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain mapping data shown in Figure 3.

claim: None of the GRA18 fragments tested other than the full-length protein could support the interactions with GSK3 in the Y2H assay.
source: None of the GRA18 fragments tested other than the full-length protein could support the interactions with GSK3 in this assay, suggesting that binding to GSK3 necessitates a larger contact surface on GRA18 than the other partners.
evidence: The claim is supported by Y2H data and leads to an inference about GSK3 binding requirements.

claim: Binding to GSK3 necessitates a larger contact surface on GRA18 than the other partners.
source: None of the GRA18 fragments tested other than the full-length protein could support the interactions with GSK3 in this assay, suggesting that binding to GSK3 necessitates a larger contact surface on GRA18 than the other partners.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the Y2H data showing only full-length GRA18 binds GSK3.

claim: The GRA18 C-terminal region mediates the interaction with both the phosphatase and the kinase.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the GRA18 C-terminal region mediates the interaction with both the phosphatase and the kinase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the biochemical data showing GRA18Ct retains binding to both GSK3β and PP2A-B56.

claim: β-catenin regulates the transcription of the Wnt target genes.
source: Indeed, β-catenin regulates the transcription of the Wnt target genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-catenin function in the Wnt pathway.

claim: In the absence of Wnt signaling, the destruction complex efficiently captures cytoplasmic β-catenin, leading to its phosphorylation by GSK3 and recognition by the β-TrCP ubiquitin ligase for degradation by the 26S proteasome.
source: In the absence of Wnt signaling, the destruction complex efficiently captures cytoplasmic β-catenin, leading to its phosphorylation by GSK3 and recognition by the β-TrCP ubiquitin ligase for degradation by the 26S proteasome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the β-catenin destruction complex mechanism.

claim: Wnt ligands trigger functional inactivation of the destruction complex, with ensuing escape of β-catenin from degradation, resulting in β-catenin accumulation and nuclear internalization.
source: Wnt ligands trigger functional inactivation of the destruction complex, with ensuing escape of β-catenin from degradation, resulting in β-catenin accumulation and nuclear internalization (Clevers, 2006; Li et al., 2012; Taelman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established studies on Wnt signaling.

claim: Parasites knockout for GRA18 did not show any obvious growth phenotype in cell culture.
source: To test this hypothesis, we generated parasites knockout for GRA18 (Figure 4A and B) in different strain types (Pru ku80 Δgra18 and 76K Δgra18) which did not show any obvious growth phenotype in cell culture (Figure 4C and data not shown), and a somewhat reduced virulence phenotype in mice when challenged by intraperitoneal injection (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GRA18 knockout parasites showed a somewhat reduced virulence phenotype in mice when challenged by intraperitoneal injection.
source: To test this hypothesis, we generated parasites knockout for GRA18 (Figure 4A and B) in different strain types (Pru ku80 Δgra18 and 76K Δgra18) which did not show any obvious growth phenotype in cell culture (Figure 4C and data not shown), and a somewhat reduced virulence phenotype in mice when challenged by intraperitoneal injection (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: β-catenin signals remained unaffected upon T. gondii infection of both human (HFF) and murine (L929) cells regardless of the GRA18 status.
source: While assessing β-catenin amounts and subcellular localization we showed that β-catenin signals remained unaffected upon T. gondii infection of both human (HFF) and murine (L929) cells regardless of the GRA18 status (Figure 4E and F, compare Pru ku80 with Δgra18).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: When parasites expressed high levels of GRA18, β-catenin signals drastically increased in cells infected by the GRA18+++ strain compared to uninfected cells.
source: Intriguingly, when parasites expressed high levels of GRA18, referred to as GRA18+++, β-catenin signals drastically increased in cells infected by the GRA18+++ strain compared to uninfected cells (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: β-catenin upregulation is associated with a strong accumulation of β-catenin in the host nuclei suggesting that a transcriptionally active bulk of β-catenin was produced.
source: β-Catenin upregulation is associated with a strong accumulation of β-catenin in the host nuclei suggesting that a transcriptionally active bulk of β-catenin was produced (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F and inference about transcriptional activity.

claim: Induction of GRA18 expression with tetracycline promoted the accumulation of β-catenin to levels comparable to those obtained with Wnt3A.
source: Induction of GRA18 expression with tetracycline promoted the accumulation of β-catenin, indicating that GRA18 alone was sufficient to drive β-catenin upregulation to levels comparable to those obtained with Wnt3A (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: GRA18 alone was sufficient to drive β-catenin upregulation.
source: Induction of GRA18 expression with tetracycline promoted the accumulation of β-catenin, indicating that GRA18 alone was sufficient to drive β-catenin upregulation to levels comparable to those obtained with Wnt3A (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data from ectopic expression in Figure 4G.

claim: GRA18 functions as a positive regulator of β-catenin.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that GRA18, very likely through the interactions with GSK3 and PP2A-B56, functions as a positive regulator of β-catenin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing GRA18 increases β-catenin levels.

claim: Thirty-eight genes were significantly and differentially regulated with most corresponding to genes up-regulated upon macrophage infection by wild-type parasites, but not with the Δgra18 strain.
source: Thirty-eight genes were significantly and differentially regulated with most corresponding to genes up-regulated upon macrophage infection by wild-type parasites, but not with the Δgra18 strain as revealed by hierarchical clustering (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Complementation of Δgra18 mutation with GRA18-HF under the control of the GRA1 promoter restored the expression pattern to levels observed with wild-type parasites or even higher.
source: Complementation of Δgra18 mutation with GRA18-HF under the control of the GRA1 promoter (Δgra18, GRA18+++) restored the expression pattern to levels observed with wild-type parasites or even higher, in strong support of the GRA18-dependent induction of those genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing complementation restores gene expression.

claim: Neither Δgra18 mutation nor LPS treatment had any significant impact on T. gondii gene expression.
source: Parasite transcriptome analysis indicated that neither Δgra18 mutation nor LPS treatment had any significant impact on T. gondii gene expression and that GRA18 expression in the Pru ku80 Δgra18, GRA18+++ complemented strain was restored with a ~ 35 fold more transcript reads than in the wild-type strain (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), in line with GRA18 overexpression driven by the GRA1 strong promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by parasite RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GRA18 expression in the Pru ku80 Δgra18, GRA18+++ complemented strain was restored with a ~ 35 fold more transcript reads than in the wild-type strain.
source: Parasite transcriptome analysis indicated that neither Δgra18 mutation nor LPS treatment had any significant impact on T. gondii gene expression and that GRA18 expression in the Pru ku80 Δgra18, GRA18+++ complemented strain was restored with a ~ 35 fold more transcript reads than in the wild-type strain (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), in line with GRA18 overexpression driven by the GRA1 strong promoter.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The expression pattern of the host genes regulated by GRA18 remained similarly regulated in the infected macrophages subjected to LPS stimulation.
source: It is noteworthy that the expression pattern of the aforementioned host genes regulated by GRA18 remained similarly regulated in the infected macrophages subjected to LPS stimulation (Figure 5A and B and Supplementary file 3), indicating that LPS did not affect GRA18 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing LPS-treated and untreated samples.

claim: LPS did not affect GRA18 function.
source: It is noteworthy that the expression pattern of the aforementioned host genes regulated by GRA18 remained similarly regulated in the infected macrophages subjected to LPS stimulation (Figure 5A and B and Supplementary file 3), indicating that LPS did not affect GRA18 function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing similar GRA18-dependent gene expression with or without LPS.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis highlighted pathways significantly affected in a GRA18-dependent fashion with functions related to the inflammatory response (e.g., Csf1, Olr1, and Tnfrsf9) and chemotaxis (e.g., Ccr7, Ccl1, Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24).
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) highlighted pathways significantly affected in a GRA18-dependent fashion (p values < 0.05) with functions related to the inflammatory response (e.g., Csf1, Olr1, and Tnfrsf9) and chemotaxis (e.g., Ccr7, Ccl1, Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: None of the typical Wnt/β-catenin target genes were found differentially regulated by GRA18.
source: Surprisingly, none of the typical Wnt/β-catenin target genes were found differentially regulated by GRA18 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 3), suggesting either that murine macrophages have a peculiar repertoire of β-catenin target genes or that GRA18 fosters a singular β-catenin transcriptional activity or that its action is independent of β-catenin.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis reproducibly demonstrated a pronounced decrease in Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 expression from cells infected with Δgra18 mutant parasites when compared to wild-type Pru or Pru Δgra18, GRA18+++ parasites.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR analysis reproducibly demonstrated a pronounced decrease in Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 expression from cells infected with Δgra18 mutant parasites when compared to wild-type Pru or Pru Δgra18, GRA18+++ parasites (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GRA18 clearly plays a major role in regulating CCL17 and CCL22 synthesis and secretion since its loss significantly lowered protein levels in the supernatant of mouse macrophages.
source: GRA18 clearly plays a major role in regulating CCL17 and CCL22 synthesis and secretion since its loss significantly lowered protein levels in the supernatant of mouse macrophages (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cells harboring insertion/deletion (indel) mutations at the Ctnnb1 locus lack β-catenin expression when compared to the wild-type parental cell line.
source: Cells harboring insertion/deletion (indel) mutations at the Ctnnb1 locus lack β-catenin expression when compared to the wild-type parental cell line (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA sequencing and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Treatment of the Ctnnb1-/- mutant cells with the GSK3 inhibitors did not lead to β-catenin expression, otherwise induced in the wild-type parental cell line.
source: As expected, treatment of the Ctnnb1-/- mutant cells with the GSK3 inhibitors did not lead to β-catenin expression, otherwise induced in the wild-type parental cell line.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data showing no β-catenin induction in mutant cells.

claim: The ectopic expression of GRA18 in RAW264.7 macrophages caused a significant increase in endogenous β-catenin.
source: The ectopic expression of GRA18 in RAW264.7 macrophages caused a significant increase in endogenous β-catenin (Figure 6C and D, compare the effect of mCherry with GRA18 expression), similarly to the effect of GRA18 when delivered by the parasites in HFF or L929 cells (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: No β-catenin was detected upon ectopic expression of GRA18 in RAW264.7 macrophages whose Ctnnb1 alleles are disrupted.
source: As expected for RAW264.7 macrophages whose Ctnnb1 alleles are disrupted, no β-catenin was detected upon ectopic expression of GRA18 (Figure 6C and D) in contrast to the significant amounts of nuclear β-catenin found in wild-type RAW264.7 macrophages expressing GRA18.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 were selectively induced in GRA18-expressing wild-type RAW264.7 macrophages when compared to mock transfected cells.
source: In the same line Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 were selectively induced in GRA18-expressing wild-type RAW264.7 macrophages when compared to mock - that is, mCherry - transfected cells (Figure 6D and E) whereas Ccl17 and Ccl24 were no longer induced in the β-catenin lacking ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ccl17 and Ccl24 were no longer induced in the β-catenin lacking RAW264.7 cells expressing GRA18.
source: In the same line Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 were selectively induced in GRA18-expressing wild-type RAW264.7 macrophages when compared to mock - that is, mCherry - transfected cells (Figure 6D and E) whereas Ccl17 and Ccl24 were no longer induced in the β-catenin lacking ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The slight reduction of Ccl22 expression in the GRA18-expressing mutant RAW264.7 macrophages suggests a different mode of regulation for the three chemokines.
source: The slight reduction of Ccl22 expression in the GRA18-expressing mutant RAW264.7 macrophages (Figure 6E) suggests a different mode of regulation for the three chemokines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing differential effects on Ccl22 versus Ccl17/Ccl24.

claim: β-catenin was required for full induction of the Ccl17 chemokine upon infection.
source: While β-catenin was required for full induction of the Ccl17 chemokine, Ccl22 expression remained unaffected in Ctnnb1-/- mutant host cells (Figure 6F), again consistent with a different mode of regulation orchestrating Ccl17 and Ccl22 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from infected cells shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ccl22 expression remained unaffected in Ctnnb1-/- mutant host cells upon infection.
source: While β-catenin was required for full induction of the Ccl17 chemokine, Ccl22 expression remained unaffected in Ctnnb1-/- mutant host cells (Figure 6F), again consistent with a different mode of regulation orchestrating Ccl17 and Ccl22 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from infected cells shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Expression of GRA18Nt, which no longer interacts with GSK3 and PP2A-B56, failed to induce β-catenin and accordingly chemokine transcripts.
source: While expression of GRA18FL in RAW264.7 macrophages caused a significant increase in endogenous β-catenin protein levels, leading to the expression of the downstream chemokines (Figure 7A and B), expression of GRA18Nt, which no longer interacts with GSK3 and PP2A-B56 (Figure 3), failed to induce β-catenin and accordingly chemokine transcripts.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: GRA18Ct, shown previously to interact with GSK3 and PP2A-B56, has retained full activity on β-catenin and downstream transcriptional consequences.
source: In contrast, GRA18Ct, shown previously to interact with GSK3 and PP2A-B56 (Figure 3) has retained full activity on β-catenin and downstream transcriptional consequences, further confirming the pivotal role of β-catenin in driving the expression of the aforementioned chemokines.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Direct interaction between GRA18 and β-catenin seems to be dispensable for GRA18's effect on β-catenin protein levels.
source: While the effect of GRA18 on β-catenin protein levels required interactions with GSK3 and/or PP2A-B56, direct interaction between GRA18 and β-catenin seems to be dispensable.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing GRA18Ct (which doesn't bind β-catenin directly) retains full activity.

claim: Treatment of RAW264.7 cells with the GSK3 inhibitors CHIR and BIO led to β-catenin protein accumulation and Ccl22 and Ccl24 upregulation.
source: Additional evidence for this model is the expression of Ccl22 and Ccl24 induced by GSK3 inhibitors in a manner that resembles the effect of GRA18 (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: GRA18 might be processed by the aspartic protease TgASP5.
source: The presence of the TEXEL motif suggests that GRA18 might be processed by the aspartic protease TgASP5, an enzyme we and others have recently shown to mediate the secretion or export of a number of GRA proteins (Coffey et al., 2015; Curt-Varesano et al., 2016; Hammoudi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of TEXEL motif and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GRA18 was no longer detected in the cytoplasm of cells invaded by TgASP5 mutant parasites.
source: As expected for a TgASP5-dependent export, GRA18 was no longer detected in the cytoplasm of cells invaded by TgASP5 mutant parasites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and accordingly, TgASP5 and GRA18 mutant parasites showed similar inability to induce target genes in macrophages ((Hammoudi et al., 2015), Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TgASP5 and GRA18 mutant parasites showed similar inability to induce target genes in macrophages.
source: As expected for a TgASP5-dependent export, GRA18 was no longer detected in the cytoplasm of cells invaded by TgASP5 mutant parasites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and accordingly, TgASP5 and GRA18 mutant parasites showed similar inability to induce target genes in macrophages ((Hammoudi et al., 2015), Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and citation to Hammoudi et al., 2015.

claim: β-catenin is a dual function co-activator protein with distinct pools serving cell-cell adhesion and gene transcription functions, respectively.
source: β-Catenin is a dual function co-activator protein with distinct pools serving cell-cell adhesion and gene transcription functions, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-catenin function.

claim: β-catenin was originally identified as an element of the adherent junction complex together with cadherin and α-catenin.
source: β-Catenin was originally identified as an element of the adherent junction complex together with cadherin and α-catenin, the latter binding to actin filaments in a process that promotes cell–cell contacts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-catenin's role in cell adhesion.

claim: A nonjunctional pool of cytoplasmic β-catenin was recognized as a transcriptional coactivator of Wnt canonical signaling pathway.
source: Further, a nonjunctional pool of cytoplasmic β-catenin was recognized as a transcriptional coactivator of Wnt canonical signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-catenin's role in Wnt signaling.

claim: Mutation in any of the β-catenin destruction complex components (APC, Axin, or β-catenin) leads to inappropriate stabilization of β-catenin, which results in cancer, most notably of the colon.
source: Mutation in any of these components (APC, Axin, or β-catenin) leads to inappropriate stabilization of β-catenin, which results in cancer, most notably of the colon (Stamos and Weis, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stamos and Weis, 2013.

claim: Axin is typified by intrinsically disordered and flexible regions that mediate direct interactions with all other core components of the destruction complex (β-catenin, APC, and GSK3).
source: Axin, a central scaffold protein of the complex, is typified by intrinsically disordered and flexible regions that mediate direct interactions with all other core components of the destruction complex (β-catenin, APC, and GSK3) (Stamos and Weis, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stamos and Weis, 2013.

claim: The T. gondii tachyzoite GRA18 carries significant disordered regions which could confer the potential of competing with Axin/APC for binding to β-catenin, GSK3, and PP2A-B56.
source: Remarkably, the T. gondii tachyzoite GRA18 also carries significant disordered regions (Figure 1E) which could confer the potential of competing with Axin/APC for binding to β-catenin, GSK3, and PP2A-B56.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the structural similarity between GRA18 and Axin.

claim: By disrupting the β-catenin destruction complex GRA18 would likely promote the stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin and ultimately β-catenin-dependent gene expression.
source: Accordingly, by disrupting the β-catenin destruction complex GRA18 would likely promote the stabilization and nuclear translocation of β-catenin and ultimately β-catenin-dependent gene expression (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: RNA-Seq performed on BMDMs indicated that β-catenin transcripts remained unaffected by GRA18.
source: RNA-Seq performed on BMDMs indicated that β-catenin transcripts remained unaffected by GRA18 (Supplementary file 3), which is consistent with a post-transcriptional regulation of β-catenin.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and leads to inference about post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: GRA18 did not alter the phospho-Ser21/Ser9 levels of GSK3.
source: Because GRA18 did not alter the phospho-Ser21/Ser9 levels (Figures 6D and 7A), we conclude that the parasite protein, which we found to bind GSK3 and inhibit its pro-degradative activity on cytoplasmic β-catenin, acts independently of the phosphorylation status of Ser21/Ser9.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 6D and 7A.

claim: GRA18 acts independently of the phosphorylation status of GSK3 Ser21/Ser9.
source: Because GRA18 did not alter the phospho-Ser21/Ser9 levels (Figures 6D and 7A), we conclude that the parasite protein, which we found to bind GSK3 and inhibit its pro-degradative activity on cytoplasmic β-catenin, acts independently of the phosphorylation status of Ser21/Ser9.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunoblot data showing no change in GSK3 phosphorylation.

claim: GRA18 carries two LxxIxE motifs within an intrinsically disordered region of the C-terminal domain.
source: Interestingly, GRA18 carries two LxxIxE motifs within an intrinsically disordered region of the C-terminal domain, which is in agreement with the B56 binding assays (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and binding data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The chemokines Ccl17, Ccl22, and Ccl24 have been found repeatedly induced by T. gondii tachyzoites regardless of the strain type in murine macrophages.
source: Those genes have been found repeatedly induced by T. gondii tachyzoites regardless of the strain type in murine macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Hammoudi et al., 2015; Melo et al., 2013; Morgado et al., 2011), as expected from the overall conservation of GRA18 across the Toxoplasma lineages.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Human placental cells have the unique ability to resist to T. gondii infection.
source: Interestingly, the human placental cells, which have the unique ability to resist to T. gondii infection, were shown to specifically respond to the invader by producing the CCL22 chemokine (Ander et al., 2018), whereas other cell types such as human fibroblasts did not ((Ander et al., 2018) and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ander et al., 2018.

claim: Human placental cells specifically respond to T. gondii by producing the CCL22 chemokine.
source: Interestingly, the human placental cells, which have the unique ability to resist to T. gondii infection, were shown to specifically respond to the invader by producing the CCL22 chemokine (Ander et al., 2018), whereas other cell types such as human fibroblasts did not ((Ander et al., 2018) and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ander et al., 2018.

claim: A quite substantial residual activation of Ccl17, and Ccl22 was observed in the absence of GRA18, which suggests that an alternative mechanism of activation by the parasites exists.
source: It is noteworthy that a quite substantial residual activation of Ccl17, and Ccl22 was observed in the absence of GRA18 (Figures 5E–F and and 6F), which suggests that an alternative mechanism of activation by the parasites exists.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing partial chemokine induction even without GRA18.

claim: Activation of β-catenin promotes differentiation and activation of dendritic cells to stimulate regulatory T cells (Tregs) and suppresses the inflammatory response.
source: For instance, activation of β-catenin promotes differentiation and activation of dendritic cells to stimulate regulatory T cells (Tregs) and suppresses the inflammatory response (Manicassamy et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2009), while β-catenin accumulation triggered by GSK3 inhibitors enables Treg cell survival (Ding et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manicassamy et al., 2010 and Zhou et al., 2009.

claim: β-catenin accumulation triggered by GSK3 inhibitors enables Treg cell survival.
source: For instance, activation of β-catenin promotes differentiation and activation of dendritic cells to stimulate regulatory T cells (Tregs) and suppresses the inflammatory response (Manicassamy et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2009), while β-catenin accumulation triggered by GSK3 inhibitors enables Treg cell survival (Ding et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ding et al., 2008.

claim: CCL17, CCL22 and CCL24 are expressed by alternatively activated M2-polarized macrophages or tolerant macrophages.
source: Interestingly, CCL17, CCL22 and CCL24 are expressed by alternatively activated M2-polarized macrophages or tolerant macrophages and the release of these chemokines results in the recruitment of Treg cells and amplification of a Th2 response (Biswas and Mantovani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Biswas and Mantovani, 2010.

claim: The release of CCL17, CCL22 and CCL24 chemokines results in the recruitment of Treg cells and amplification of a Th2 response.
source: Interestingly, CCL17, CCL22 and CCL24 are expressed by alternatively activated M2-polarized macrophages or tolerant macrophages and the release of these chemokines results in the recruitment of Treg cells and amplification of a Th2 response (Biswas and Mantovani, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Biswas and Mantovani, 2010.
